title: Fire Safety Awareness
body: Fire is one of those things we hope we'll never have to deal with — but if it happens, the seconds count and there's no time to start wondering what to do. That's why every single one of us needs to know the plan. At Black Horse Beamish our assembly point is the car park at the bottom of the Orangery. Whatever happens, that's where we all head to be counted.

If YOU discover a fire, don't tackle it first — raise the alarm straight away by operating the nearest break-glass call point, start moving guests calmly towards the nearest fire exit, and call 999. Only ever attempt to put a fire out if it's small, you've been trained, and your escape route is behind you. If in any doubt at all, just get out.

If you HEAR the alarm, treat it as the real thing every time — never assume it's a test. Stop what you're doing, help guests to the nearest exit, and go. Don't use the lifts, and definitely don't stop to grab your coat or your phone. Close doors behind you as you leave — it slows the spread of fire and smoke and can buy people vital time.

Once you're out, stay out. The Duty Manager runs the roll call and deals with the Fire Service, so report to them at the assembly point. Nobody goes back inside for any reason until the Fire Service or Duty Manager says it's safe. And day to day? Keep fire doors closed (never wedged open) and keep exits and escape routes clear — a blocked exit could cost a life.

title: Allergen Awareness
body: For most people a meal out is a treat — but for someone with a food allergy, the wrong dish can be life-threatening. A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can come on in minutes and can be fatal. That's why allergens are taken so seriously in law, and why getting it right is one of the most important things we do.

There are 14 allergens that must be declared by law: celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide (sulphites) and tree nuts. You don't have to memorise every dish — but you DO have to know where to find the accurate allergen information and use it every single time.

The golden rule is simple: never guess. If a guest tells you about an allergy, take it seriously, tell a chef or supervisor straight away, and check the allergen information before you promise anything. If you can't be certain a dish is safe for that guest, don't serve it. It really is better to take an extra two minutes than to take a risk with someone's life.

Watch out for cross-contamination too — an allergen can transfer onto an otherwise 'free-from' dish through shared boards, utensils, fryers or hands. Allergen orders should be prepared separately and carefully. Remember 'Natasha's Law' means pre-packed-for-direct-sale food needs full ingredient labelling. When in doubt, always check — the guest is trusting us with their health.

title: Challenge 25 & Age-Restricted Sales
body: Selling alcohol is a privilege that comes with real responsibility. It is a criminal offence to sell alcohol to anyone under 18 — and it's not just the business that's on the line. The person who makes the sale can be personally fined, and a personal licence holder can lose their licence. So this one really matters for you as well as for us.

That's where Challenge 25 comes in. The idea is simple: if a customer looks under 25, you ask for ID before serving them alcohol. Someone who's genuinely 18 won't mind proving it — and it gives you a comfortable margin. If they can't prove they're 18 or over, you politely refuse. No ID, no sale. It's as clear as that.

Only accept valid photo ID: a photo driving licence, a passport, or a card carrying the PASS hologram. Check the photo really is them, check the date of birth, and make sure the ID looks genuine and hasn't been tampered with. Watch out for 'proxy' sales too — an adult buying alcohol to pass to an under-18. If you spot it, refuse the sale.

Every time you refuse a sale, record it in the refusals log — it protects you and shows we take our licence seriously. If a customer gets pushy after a refusal, don't feel you have to back down or handle it alone: call a manager. When you're unsure about someone's age, the safe answer is always to ask for ID, or ask a manager.

title: Manual Handling — Moving Kegs & Casks
body: Bad backs are one of the most common reasons people take time off work, and across the UK musculoskeletal injuries account for roughly a third of all workplace ill-health. In a busy cellar full of heavy kegs, that's a real risk — a full 50-litre keg can weigh over 70kg, which is far too much to be throwing around without thinking.

Before you lift anything, run through T.I.L.E. in your head: the Task (what am I moving and where to?), the Individual (am I fit to do this, do I need help?), the Load (how heavy and awkward is it?) and the Environment (is the floor wet, is the ramp clear, is it well lit?). Ten seconds of thinking prevents a lot of injuries.

When you do lift, use good technique: get close to the load, bend your knees rather than your back, keep your back straight, and lift smoothly. Never twist while you're carrying weight — move your feet instead. For full kegs, don't be a hero: use a sack barrow or keg trolley, or get a colleague to help with a two-person lift.

Kegs can also be rolled or 'walked' — but always in a slow, controlled way so one never gets away from you. Keep cellar drops, ramps and hatches clear, dry and well lit, and take your time on the steps. If something feels too heavy or awkward, stop and get help. Protecting your back today keeps you working pain-free for years to come.

title: Safe Knife Use
body: Knives are the most-used tool in any kitchen, and used well they're perfectly safe. But a moment's carelessness can cause a nasty cut that puts you out of action and leaves the team short. The good news is that almost every knife injury is avoidable if you follow a few simple habits.

It sounds backwards, but a sharp knife is actually SAFER than a blunt one. A sharp blade cuts cleanly with little pressure, whereas a blunt knife needs force and is far more likely to slip. Always use the right knife for the job, and always cut on a stable, non-slip board — pop a damp cloth underneath if it's sliding around.

Protect your fingers with the 'claw' grip: curl your fingertips under and let your knuckles guide the blade. Always cut down and away from your body, never towards your hand. Keep your eyes on what you're doing — this is not the moment for a chat over your shoulder.

Carry a knife point-down by your side, and warn people if you're moving through the kitchen. Never leave a knife in a sink of water where someone could grab it by the blade, and never try to catch a falling knife — step back and let it drop, then pick it up. Wash and store knives safely as soon as you've finished with them.

title: Slips, Trips & Falls
body: Did you know that slips, trips and falls are the single most common cause of accidents in hospitality businesses, making up around 30% of all workplace injuries? Who knew that simply walking around could be so risky! They're also the most common cause of major injuries — think broken bones and nasty sprains — in our industry.

It matters because these accidents hurt real people: our guests, our colleagues and ourselves. Across the UK they lead to hundreds of thousands of lost working days every year and cost businesses more than £500 million. Behind every one of those numbers is someone in pain and a team left short-handed.

So how do we stay safe? The most important thing is to be vigilant — keep your eyes open and actually DO SOMETHING about any hazard you spot. Someone left a spill on the kitchen floor? Do something! A vacuum cleaner left out with its power lead trailing across a corridor? Do something! Don't assume it's someone else's job.

The first step is always to make the area safe: grab a wet floor sign and pop it over a spillage, mop it up, or move that trailing cable or box out of the walkway. Once you're sure it's safe, the second step is just as important — tell your line manager. We need to know a hazard was there so we can look into why, and stop it happening again. Good footwear (non-slip, closed-toe), clear walkways, good lighting and cleaning up as you go all help too.

title: Accident & Near-Miss Reporting
body: Here's a question: if someone slips on a wet floor but catches themselves and isn't hurt, is it worth mentioning? Absolutely yes! That's what we call a 'near-miss' — an event that could have caused harm but didn't, this time. Near-misses are basically free warnings, and reporting them is one of the smartest things we can do.

The reason is simple. Behind most serious accidents there were usually lots of near-misses first. If we hear about the near-miss — the spill that nearly caused a fall, the box that nearly fell off a shelf — we can fix the cause before anyone actually gets hurt. Report the small stuff, and we prevent the big stuff.

So please report ALL accidents and near-misses, however minor they seem. If someone is hurt, deal with that first: make the area safe and get first aid. Then tell the Duty Manager and make sure it's written up in the accident book before the end of your shift, while it's still fresh in everyone's mind.

One more thing that's really important: there is NO blame for reporting. We're not looking for someone to point the finger at — we're looking to learn and improve so it doesn't happen again. If it's a serious emergency, call 999 straight away. Honest, prompt reporting keeps everyone safer, and that includes you.

title: Hazard Spotting
body: A hazard is simply anything with the potential to cause harm — and once you start looking, they're everywhere: a spill, a trailing cable, a wobbly shelf, a blocked fire exit, a frayed plug, a chemical left out. The skill of hazard spotting is training your eyes to notice these things before they cause an accident, not after.

The trick is to look up, down and around as you move through your area, rather than switching onto autopilot. A great habit is to ask yourself, 'if a guest walked through here right now, what might hurt them?' You know your own work area better than anyone, so you're actually the best-placed person to spot when something isn't right.

Spotting a hazard is only half the job — the other half is doing something about it. If you can deal with it safely and quickly, do so: mop the spill, coil the cable, move the box. If you can't fix it safely yourself (say, a faulty appliance or damaged flooring), take it out of use if you can and report it.

The one thing you must never do is walk past a hazard thinking 'someone else will sort that out.' That someone is you. It takes moments to make something safe or to flag it, and it could save a colleague or guest from a serious injury. Reporting hazards early is how we stop accidents before they ever happen.

title: COSHH — Safe Use of Chemicals
body: We use cleaning chemicals all day, every day — sanitisers, degreasers, descalers, glasswash detergent — and it's easy to forget that some of them are genuinely hazardous. COSHH stands for the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health, and it's the law that makes sure we use these products safely. Get it right and they're a great help; get it wrong and they can burn skin, damage eyes or release toxic fumes.

The single most important rule is one you may have heard before: never mix chemicals. Mixing bleach with an acidic cleaner, for example, can release toxic chlorine gas that can seriously harm you in seconds. Only ever use approved products for the job, and always follow the label and the COSHH assessment for the right dilution and method.

Wear the PPE that's provided — usually gloves, and eye protection for stronger products — and make sure there's decent ventilation. Store chemicals properly: labelled, in their original containers, and well away from food. And here's a big one: NEVER decant a chemical into a drinks bottle or an unlabelled container. People have been seriously poisoned that way.

If there's a spill, a splash to the skin or eyes, or you feel unwell, act straight away — rinse, get first aid, and report it. The COSHH information and safety data sheets should be easy to find for everyone who needs them. If you ever come across an unlabelled container, don't use it and don't guess what's in it — report it.

title: Cross-Contamination Prevention
body: Cross-contamination is one of the biggest causes of food poisoning, and it happens when harmful bacteria (or allergens) are transferred from one food, surface or hand to another. The classic example is juices from raw chicken getting onto a salad that won't be cooked — the cooking would have killed the bacteria on the chicken, but the salad goes out raw and makes someone ill.

The main defence is separation: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods well apart at every stage. Use the colour-coded chopping boards and equipment correctly (red for raw meat, green for salad and fruit, and so on), and never let a board or knife used for raw meat touch ready-to-eat food without a proper wash first.

Your hands are one of the most common ways bacteria travel around a kitchen, so wash them thoroughly and often — especially after handling raw meat, taking out waste, or touching your face. Clean and sanitise surfaces and equipment between different tasks, and don't use the same cloth on raw-meat areas and then on a salad prep bench.

Storage matters too. Always keep raw meat and poultry stored below ready-to-eat foods in the fridge, so nothing can drip down and contaminate them. A few good habits — separate, clean hands, colour-coding and correct storage — stop cross-contamination in its tracks and keep our guests safe.

title: Personal Hygiene & Handwashing
body: It's not glamorous, but good personal hygiene is one of the most powerful tools we have for keeping guests safe from illness — and handwashing is right at the top of the list. Our hands touch everything, which means they can carry bacteria from a door handle or a raw ingredient straight onto a plate of food if we're not careful.

So wash your hands properly and often. 'Properly' means soap and warm water, scrubbing all over — palms, backs, between the fingers and thumbs — for at least 20 seconds, then drying them. Wash after using the toilet, after handling raw food or waste, after touching your face or hair, and whenever you start a new task.

Beyond hands, keep the whole picture tidy: nails short and clean with no varnish or false nails in food areas, hair tied back or covered, and any cuts covered with a blue (detectable) plaster so it's easy to spot if one comes off. Strong perfume or aftershave is best avoided around food, and jewellery should be kept to a minimum.

Crucially, if you're ill — especially with vomiting or diarrhoea — you must report it and stay away from food. The rule is to be symptom-free for at least 48 hours before you handle food again. It might feel like you're letting the team down, but coming in could put dozens of guests at risk. When in doubt, speak to your manager.

title: GDPR & Data Protection
body: Every day we handle personal information — guest names, phone numbers, card details, booking notes, wedding plans, and staff records. Data protection law (UK GDPR) exists to make sure we look after all of that responsibly. It's not just red tape: a data breach can cause real harm to real people and can land the business with a large fine.

The first principle is 'need to know'. Only access personal information you actually need to do your job — never out of curiosity, and never to look up a friend, a celebrity guest or an ex. Keep what you see confidential; guest and colleague information is not something to gossip about or share on social media.

Keep information secure in practical ways: lock away paperwork like booking sheets and function orders, use strong passwords, and lock your screen when you step away. Be careful with emails — sending guest details to the wrong person is one of the most common breaches there is, so always double-check the address before you hit send.

If something goes wrong — a lost booking book, a laptop left on a train, an email to the wrong guest — report it to the General Manager straight away. Quick reporting lets us limit the damage. And if a guest ever asks to see the information we hold about them, don't guess — pass the request to the General Manager to handle properly.

title: Spotting Drug Use in Customers
body: Nobody likes to think about it, but drug use can happen in any licensed venue, and part of protecting our guests and our licence is knowing how to spot it and respond calmly. It's not about playing detective — it's about being aware, keeping people safe, and passing concerns to a manager.

There are some common signs worth knowing. In a person, watch for very frequent trips to the toilet (especially in pairs), over-excitable or jittery behaviour, unusual paranoia or aggression, glazed eyes or nosebleeds. In the venue, look out for tampering in the toilets, powder residue on surfaces or cisterns, or drugs and paraphernalia left behind.

If you suspect drug use, the key thing is do NOT confront or search the person — that could put you in danger and isn't your job. Instead, quietly inform the Duty Manager and let them decide what to do. Keep an eye on the person's welfare, because their safety matters even if they've broken the rules.

Practically, we'd usually refuse further alcohol service to someone we believe is under the influence of drugs, and monitor the situation. Make a note of what you actually saw — facts, not guesses — because the manager may need to record it or involve the police. Above all: guest safety first, protect our licence, and let a manager lead the response.

title: Manual Handling — Flipping & Turning Mattresses
body: Turning and flipping mattresses is a routine part of keeping our rooms in top condition — but it's also a sneaky cause of back, shoulder and wrist strain. Mattresses are heavy, floppy and awkward to grip, which is exactly the combination that catches people out. A little technique goes a long way.

Wherever possible, make it a two-person job. Two people sharing the load can turn a mattress smoothly and safely, whereas one person wrestling with it alone is asking for a pulled muscle. Before you start, clear the area around the bed so you're not tripping or knocking into furniture as you move.

Use good lifting basics: get a firm grip (using the handles if the mattress has them), bend your knees rather than your back, keep your back straight, and move your feet to turn rather than twisting your spine. Don't try to lift the whole dead weight in one go — push, roll and turn it in stages, letting the bed take the weight.

If you feel any strain or a twinge, stop — don't try to push through it. Report it, and get help before carrying on. Awkward, heavy tasks like this are far safer shared, so never feel you have to struggle on alone just to save time. Looking after your body is what keeps you able to do the job.

title: Manual Handling — Moving Tables & Furniture
body: Setting up and turning around function rooms means shifting a LOT of tables, chairs and furniture — often against the clock before a wedding or event. That time pressure is exactly when people rush, lift badly and hurt themselves. A calm, planned approach keeps you injury-free and actually gets the room ready faster.

Before you lift, check the weight and think it through. Heavy round tables and stacks of chairs are two-person jobs or trolley jobs — don't try to prove a point by hauling them solo. Plan your route first so it's clear, dry and free of trip hazards, and know where the item is going before you pick it up.

Use the basics every time: keep the load close to your body, bend your knees not your back, keep your back straight, and never twist — move your feet to turn instead. Watch your fingers and toes when you set things down, and put items down squarely and under control rather than dropping them the last few inches.

When you stack chairs or store furniture, keep stacks at a safe height so they don't topple, and never block fire exits or walkways with stored gear, even 'just for a minute'. Don't overload trolleys either. Pace yourself through a big set-up — spreading the effort protects your back and keeps the whole team going strong all day.

title: Ladder & Step-Ladder Safety
body: Ladders and step-ladders are handy, but they're involved in a surprising number of serious workplace falls every year — and a fall from even a low height can break bones. The first question to ask is whether you even need a ladder: for very quick, light jobs they're fine, but for anything longer or higher, a proper platform or tower is safer.

If a ladder is the right tool, check it before you use it. Look for damage — bent stiles, cracked or missing feet, loose rungs. If it's faulty, don't use it: take it out of service and report it. Set it up on firm, level ground, and with a step-ladder make sure it's fully open and locked, never used half-folded or leaned against a wall.

While you're on it, keep three points of contact — that's two feet and a hand, or similar — and keep your body within the stiles (the side rails). The classic mistake is overreaching: if you have to lean out to reach, get down and move the ladder instead. Never stand on the very top step, and don't carry heavy or bulky items up with you.

For anything higher or more awkward, have a colleague foot the ladder to steady it, and be aware of people and doors around you. It only takes a moment to set a ladder up properly, and it's a lot quicker than recovering from a broken wrist. If access looks unsafe, stop and report it rather than taking a chance.

title: Visual Checks of Electrical Items
body: Faulty electrics cause fires and give people serious shocks — but the good news is that a huge number of electrical problems can be spotted with a simple visual check before you even switch something on. You don't need to be an electrician; you just need to know what a warning sign looks like and to act on it.

Before you use a piece of electrical equipment, take a couple of seconds to look it over. Check the cable for damage — cuts, fraying or exposed wires. Check the plug for cracks, and look for tell-tale signs of overheating like scorch marks or a brown, discoloured plug. And if you ever smell burning or hot plastic, that's an instant stop.

Also watch how things are set up. Overloaded sockets and 'daisy-chained' extension leads are a real fire risk, and cables trailing across walkways are both a trip hazard and easily damaged. Keep water and electrics well apart — never handle plugs or switches with wet hands or near a wet surface.

If an item fails your check, don't use it and don't try to fix it yourself — that's a job for a competent person. Switch it off, unplug it if safe, label it clearly as out of use so nobody else plugs it in, and report it. A ten-second look could prevent a fire or save someone from a nasty shock.

title: Clean As You Go
body: 'Clean as you go' is a phrase you'll hear constantly in hospitality, and for good reason — it's the habit of cleaning and tidying continuously while you work, rather than letting mess pile up to deal with later. It keeps your area safe, hygienic and under control, and it makes service run far more smoothly.

Think about what happens when you don't. Spills sit on the floor and become slip hazards. Dirty boards and surfaces spread bacteria and allergens. Clutter builds until you can't find anything and you're working in chaos. Then at the end of service you face a mountain of cleaning when you're already tired. Little and often is always easier.

In practice it means: wipe spills the moment they happen, clear rubbish and packaging as you create it, and clean and sanitise surfaces between tasks. Put tools, ingredients and stock back where they belong once you've finished with them, so the next person can find them and the area stays clear.

It's everyone's job, not just the cleaners' or the KP's. A clean, tidy area is safer for the whole team, more hygienic for our guests, and honestly it looks far more professional if a guest glances behind the bar or into the kitchen. Get into the habit and you'll wonder how you ever worked any other way.

title: Temperature Control — Cook, Chill, Hold
body: Temperature is one of the most powerful weapons we have against food poisoning, because it controls whether harmful bacteria multiply or are killed. The zone to fear is the 'danger zone' — roughly 8°C to 63°C — where bacteria multiply happily. Our whole job is to move food through that zone quickly and keep it out of it the rest of the time.

When cooking, get food properly hot all the way through. A core temperature of 75°C is a common target that kills the bacteria that make people ill. Use a clean, calibrated probe to check the thickest part rather than guessing by colour, and don't forget to clean and sanitise the probe between uses.

For holding food, the rules are simple: keep chilled food cold — 8°C or below by law, and we aim for 5°C or below — and keep hot food hot at 63°C or above. If you're cooling cooked food to store it, cool it quickly (ideally within about 90 minutes) and get it into the fridge, rather than leaving it sitting out in the danger zone.

Finally, don't just do it — record it. Checking and writing down temperatures for cooking, chilling and hot-holding is part of our food safety system and proves we're keeping food safe. If a fridge is running warm or food isn't reaching the right temperature, report it straight away so it can be sorted before anyone is put at risk.

title: Fridge & Freezer / Cold Chain Checks
body: The 'cold chain' is the unbroken run of cold temperatures that keeps food safe all the way from delivery to the moment it's cooked or served. Every link matters — if food warms up at any point, bacteria get the chance to multiply, and you can't always see or smell the difference. That's why daily fridge and freezer checks are so important.

At the start of each day (and often through it), check and record fridge and freezer temperatures. Fridges should be running at 5°C or below, and freezers at −18°C or below. Writing the readings down isn't box-ticking — it's how we catch a failing unit early, before a whole fridge of stock has to be thrown away or, worse, served.

How you use the units matters too. Don't overload them or block the vents, because that stops cold air circulating and creates warm spots. Keep doors closed as much as possible, and when a delivery arrives, put chilled and frozen items away quickly rather than leaving them out on the pass to warm up.

Keep raw meat stored below ready-to-eat foods so nothing drips down, and rotate stock so older items get used first. If a unit is running warm, don't ignore it — report it immediately and check the food inside, because acting fast can be the difference between a quick repair and a food-poisoning risk.

title: Complaint Handling
body: It's tempting to see a complaint as a problem, but it's actually a gift. A guest who complains is giving us the chance to put things right — and research consistently shows that a complaint handled well often leaves a guest MORE loyal than if nothing had gone wrong at all. The guests to worry about are the ones who say nothing and simply never come back.

The first and most important skill is to listen. Give the guest your full attention, let them finish without interrupting, and don't get defensive or start making excuses. Often people simply want to feel heard. Acknowledge how they feel and apologise for the experience — you can be genuinely sorry someone's evening was spoiled without arguing about who's to blame.

Then take ownership. If it's something you can put right, do it. If it's beyond what you can do, don't just pass the buck — escalate it to a manager promptly and make sure the guest knows it's being taken seriously. Never argue with a guest, and never discuss whose fault it was in front of them or other diners.

Finally, agree what happens next, follow through on it, and thank them for raising it. Some issues are urgent and must go straight to the Duty Manager — anything involving an allergic reaction, illness, injury, or a threat of legal or online action. Handle a complaint with care and you don't just fix a meal, you keep a customer.

title: 10 Steps to Great Customer Service
body: Great customer service is what turns a first-time visitor into a regular, and a good wedding into one guests talk about for years. It isn't about being posh or stuffy — it's about making every single guest feel noticed, welcome and genuinely looked after, from the moment they arrive to the moment they leave.

It starts with the basics done consistently: smile and greet people promptly, make eye contact, and be genuinely warm rather than going through the motions. Even when you're rushed off your feet, a quick 'I'll be right with you' tells a waiting guest they've been seen — being ignored is what really annoys people.

Then it's about being switched on. Know your menu so you can answer questions and make recommendations, anticipate needs before you're asked (topping up water, clearing plates), and be attentive without hovering. Handle every request positively — 'let me sort that for you' beats 'that's not my section' every time — and keep your areas clean and tidy.

And when something does go wrong, deal with it gracefully rather than getting flustered or defensive. Finish with a warm farewell and a genuine invitation to come back. String those habits together and you've got the ten steps: greet, connect, welcome, anticipate, know your stuff, be attentive, stay positive, stay tidy, recover well, and send them off happy.

title: Spotting Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE)
body: As a hotel and events venue, we have a real responsibility to help keep children safe. Child sexual exploitation (CSE) is a form of abuse where a child is manipulated or coerced into sexual activity, sometimes in places just like ours. It can be uncomfortable to think about, but being aware and knowing what to do can genuinely protect a young person.

There are signs worth being alert to. Be cautious about an adult booking a room with a child or young person who seems anxious, withdrawn, frightened or under the adult's control — particularly where there's an obvious age gap. Watch for a young person who seems out of place, has little control over their own money, phone or movements, or attempts to keep a booking secret.

If something doesn't feel right, trust that instinct — but do NOT try to investigate or confront anyone yourself. That could put you or the young person at greater risk. Instead, quietly note what you've actually seen or heard, and report it to the Duty Manager, who is responsible for deciding what happens next.

If a child appears to be in immediate danger, call 999 without delay. Keep any concern confidential and only share it with those who genuinely need to know. You don't need to be certain, and you're not expected to have all the answers — you just need to notice, and to speak up. The child's welfare always comes first.

title: Bullying & Harassment
body: Everyone at Black Horse Beamish has the right to come to work and be treated with dignity and respect — that's not a nice-to-have, it's the standard we hold each other to. Bullying and harassment have no place here, whether they come from a colleague, a manager, or even a guest.

It helps to know what we mean. Bullying is behaviour that's offensive, intimidating, malicious or humiliating — think persistent criticism, being belittled, or someone deliberately making a colleague's life difficult. Harassment is unwanted conduct that violates someone's dignity or creates a hostile, degrading or intimidating environment for them. Both can happen face to face, in messages, or online.

One important point: it's not about intention, it's about impact. 'It was just banter' isn't a defence if the behaviour is genuinely unwelcome and hurtful to the person on the receiving end. What one person finds funny, another may find deeply upsetting — and everyone's right to feel respected is what counts.

If you experience or witness bullying or harassment, please don't just ignore it and hope it goes away. You can raise it with a manager or through the grievance procedure, and it will be handled confidentially and taken seriously. Nobody who raises a genuine concern will be treated badly for doing so — speaking up is how we keep this a good place to work.

title: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace
body: Sexual harassment is unwanted conduct of a sexual nature, and it is never acceptable at Black Horse Beamish — full stop. In hospitality, with late nights, alcohol and lots of social contact, it's especially important that everyone knows where the line is and knows they'll be supported if that line is crossed.

It covers a wide range of behaviour: sexual comments or 'jokes', unwanted touching, staring or leering, sexual messages or images, spreading sexual rumours, or unwelcome advances. It can come from anyone — a colleague, a manager, a supplier, or a guest — and none of those is an exception. A customer being 'a bit handsy' is not just part of the job.

The law now places a positive duty on employers to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment, including harassment by third parties like guests. That means we actively look out for it and act on it — this isn't something anyone is expected to simply put up with. Your comfort and safety matter more than avoiding an awkward moment.

If it happens to you, or you witness it happening to someone else, please report it to a manager. You'll be listened to and supported, and no one will be victimised for raising a genuine concern. If a guest is the problem, tell a manager rather than trying to handle it alone — we would far rather lose a booking than let a colleague be harassed.

title: Equality & Diversity
body: A great hospitality team is a mix of all sorts of people, and our guests are just as varied. Equality and diversity is about treating everyone fairly and valuing those differences — among our team and towards every guest who walks through the door. It's the right thing to do, and it's also the law.

The Equality Act 2010 protects nine 'protected characteristics': age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Discrimination against someone because of any of these is unlawful. It can be direct (treating someone worse because of who they are) or indirect (a rule or practice that unfairly disadvantages a particular group).

In our world this shows up in practical ways. It means welcoming all guests equally and making reasonable adjustments — for example, being ready to read a menu aloud, welcoming an assistance dog, or finding an accessible table without fuss. It means recruiting and rostering fairly, and never letting a guest's or colleague's background affect the service or respect they get.

If you see discrimination or hear a comment that crosses the line, don't let it slide — challenge it if it's safe to, or report it. Diversity genuinely makes us a better, richer team and a more welcoming venue. Fair, respectful treatment for everyone, every time, is simply how we do things here.

title: The Perfect Serve (Bar)
body: On the bar, consistency is everything. A guest who gets a beautifully poured pint or a properly made G&T on their first visit expects exactly the same on their tenth — and if we deliver it every time, that's how we build a reputation and a loyal crowd. The 'perfect serve' is just doing the simple things right, drink after drink.

It starts with the glass. Use the correct, clean glassware for each drink, chilled where it should be, and check it's spotless and unchipped before you pour. The right glass isn't fussiness — it genuinely affects how a drink looks, smells and tastes, and a chipped glass is a safety issue that has to be binned.

Then the pour. Serve draught beer to a proper head, letting cask ales settle if they need it, and check the beer looks clear and bright before it goes out — cloudy or 'off' beer usually means a line or cellar issue to flag. Measure spirits correctly with the right measure every time (it's a legal requirement as well as good practice), and serve wine at the right temperature and measure.

Finally, presentation. Garnish and finish drinks to spec — the correct garnish, the right ice, a clean pour down the side of the glass — every single time. It only takes a few extra seconds, and it's the difference between a drink that's just wet and one a guest is genuinely pleased to be handed.

title: Cellar Safety & CO2 Awareness
body: The cellar is the engine room of the bar, but it packs several hazards into one small, cold space: heavy kegs, wet floors, and — the big one — gas. The CO2 and mixed gas we use to dispense drinks is invisible and has no real smell, but in a confined space it can build up and displace oxygen, which can cause someone to collapse or even suffocate. It's not something to be casual about.

That's why we have a gas alarm in the cellar. Know where it is and what it sounds like, and treat it deadly seriously: if the CO2 alarm goes off, do NOT go in. Get out or stay out, keep others away, and report it immediately so it can be dealt with safely. Never try to 'just nip in' to grab something while an alarm is sounding.

Good ventilation is essential, so never block vents or prop the cellar in a way that stops air moving. Change gas cylinders carefully following the correct procedure, and make sure they're secured so they can't fall. If you smell or suspect a gas leak, or a cylinder is damaged, treat it as urgent and report it.

The rest is good housekeeping: keep floors clear and dry to prevent slips, handle kegs with proper technique or a trolley, and take care on cellar steps and drops. Respect the space, respect the gas, and the cellar is a perfectly safe place to work.

title: Working at Height
body: Falls from height are the single biggest cause of workplace deaths in the UK, and they cause thousands of serious injuries every year too. And here's the sobering bit: many of those falls are from quite low heights — a step-ladder, a chair, the edge of a stage. You don't have to be up a scaffold to be at risk.

'Working at height' means any task where you could fall a distance likely to cause injury. The very first thing to ask is whether you can avoid it altogether — can the job be done from the ground, with a longer-handled tool for instance? If you must go up, use the right, well-maintained equipment for the task and never improvise.

That word 'improvise' is key. Standing on a chair, a box, a bar stool or a pile of furniture to reach something is one of the most common ways people fall — never do it. Use a proper step-ladder for short jobs or a platform/tower for longer ones, keep three points of contact, and don't overreach or overload yourself while you're up there.

Be aware of what's around and below you — other people, doors that might open, and hazards underfoot. If the access looks unsafe or you're not sure you can do it safely, stop and report it rather than taking a chance. A few minutes setting up properly is nothing compared to weeks off with a broken bone.

title: Minor Maintenance — Changing Lightbulbs
body: Changing a lightbulb sounds like the simplest job in the world — which is exactly why people get hurt doing it. It combines two hazards we've already covered, electricity and working at height, and adds a hot bulb into the mix. Slow down, and a two-minute job stays a two-minute job.

First, deal with the power. Switch the light off and, where you can, isolate it properly so it can't be turned back on while you're working. Then give a hot bulb time to cool before you touch it — a bulb that's been on can easily burn your fingers, and a startled jump up a ladder is how falls happen.

Get your access right. Use the correct step-ladder or steps for the height — never a chair, a table or a wobbly stool — and set it up on firm, level ground. If it's a high or awkward fitting, get someone to steady the ladder and keep three points of contact while you work.

Use the correct replacement — the right type, fitting and wattage — because the wrong bulb can overheat or damage the fitting. Dispose of the old bulb safely (some types, like fluorescent tubes, need special disposal). And if the fitting itself looks damaged, scorched or loose, don't force it — stop and report it to maintenance.

title: Preventing Burns & Scalds
body: A busy kitchen is full of things that are extremely hot — pans, ovens, fryers, steamers, hot water and steam — so burns and scalds are among the most common kitchen injuries. The reassuring news is that nearly all of them are preventable with a few good habits and a bit of awareness of what's going on around you.

Start with the simple stuff. Always use a DRY oven cloth — a damp or wet cloth conducts heat straight through and gives you a nasty scald. Turn pan handles inwards, away from the edge and off the flame, so they can't be knocked or catch fire. And when you open a lid or a pan, open it away from your face to let the steam escape safely.

Communication saves skin. Call out clearly when you're moving around with something hot — 'hot behind!', 'hot pan!' — so colleagues can keep clear. Take real care with hot oil and fryers, which can spit and cause serious burns, and never add wet food to hot oil. Move hot pans and stockpots slowly and deliberately.

If someone does get burned, act fast: cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 20 minutes, remove any watches or rings near the area before it swells, and don't put butter or creams on it. For anything more than a minor burn, get first aid and, if serious, medical help. Then report it so we can prevent the next one.

title: Wet Floor & Spillage Management
body: We've said it before but it's worth its own trainer: wet floors are one of the biggest causes of slips, and slips are the most common accident in our industry. A wet patch you can barely see can put a guest or colleague flat on their back in an instant. The way we deal with spills says a lot about how safe our venue really is.

The golden rule is deal with it now, not later, and never walk past it. The moment you spot a spillage, take ownership. Warn anyone nearby, put out a wet floor sign so people know, and then clean it up properly — absorb or mop the liquid and then make sure the floor is actually DRY, because a damp floor is still a slip risk.

Leave the sign in place until the floor is completely dry, then take it away — a wet floor sign left out permanently just gets ignored, so it needs to mean something. Use the right method and equipment for what's been spilled: water and drinks are one thing, but oil, grease or broken glass need extra care and the correct clean-up.

Once it's safe, mention recurring problems to your manager. If the same spot is always wet — a leaking fridge, a dripping tap, a worn mat that traps water — we need to fix the cause, not just keep mopping. Spot it, sign it, clean it, dry it, and report anything that keeps coming back.

title: Bomb Threat & Suspicious Packages
body: It's rare, thankfully, but every venue should know what to do if a bomb threat is received or a suspicious item is found. The overwhelming majority of threats turn out to be hoaxes — but we treat every one seriously, because staying calm and following a simple procedure is what keeps everyone safe.

If you take a threat over the phone, the key is to keep the caller talking for as long as you can and gather information. Don't hang up first. Note down their exact words, the time of the call, and anything you can about their voice, accent, and any background noise (traffic, music, machinery). If your phone shows the number, note it. As soon as the call ends, alert the Duty Manager immediately.

If you find a suspicious item — an unattended bag, a package that doesn't belong, something that just feels wrong — remember the phrase 'do not touch'. Don't move it, open it, cover it or investigate it. Keep people well away from it and alert the Duty Manager, who will decide on evacuation and whether to call 999.

The Duty Manager leads the response and makes the call on evacuating and contacting the police. Your job is to stay calm, record what you can, avoid touching anything suspicious, and follow instructions. Panic helps no one; a calm, practised response is what keeps guests and colleagues safe.

title: Security & Lockdown — Run, Hide, Tell
body: This is one we all hope never to use, but in the very rare event of a violent attack — someone with a weapon, for instance — the national advice is simple and easy to remember: Run, Hide, Tell. Knowing it in advance means you can act fast instead of freezing, and that can save lives, including your own.

RUN comes first. If there's a safe route away from the danger, take it — get yourself and others out and to safety. Leave your belongings behind; nothing you own is worth going back for. Encourage others to come with you, but don't waste time trying to persuade anyone who won't move.

If you can't safely run, HIDE. Get out of sight, put a solid barrier between you and the danger if you can, lock or barricade the door, and stay away from windows. Silence your phone (not just vibrate) so it doesn't give you away, and stay quiet and still until help arrives.

TELL is the final step: when it's safe to do so, call 999 and give the police whatever you know — where, what, how many attackers, what they look like. When armed police arrive, follow their instructions exactly, keep your hands visible, and don't make sudden movements. Help others stay calm, but never try to be a hero — your safety comes first.

title: First Aid Awareness
body: You don't have to be a trained first aider to be useful in an emergency — but everyone should know the basics of what to do and, crucially, who to get. Knowing where the first aid kit is and who your workplace first aiders are, before anything happens, means you won't be scrambling when seconds count.

In a serious emergency, the priority order is simple: keep yourself safe, then call 999 for help, then tell the Duty Manager. Don't move a seriously injured person unless leaving them puts them in greater danger (like a fire). Reassure them, keep them still and warm, and stay with them until help arrives.

A few basics are worth knowing. For a burn, cool it under cool running water. For heavy bleeding, apply firm, direct pressure to the wound. For choking, encourage the person to cough, and if that fails and you're trained, give back blows and abdominal thrusts. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, that's a 999 call and CPR if you're trained.

Afterwards, every incident and any first aid given must be recorded and reported — it's part of looking after people and spotting patterns. First aiders should only work within their training, and everyone else should focus on getting help quickly and keeping the casualty calm. Knowing the basics turns a bystander into a lifesaver.

title: Date Labelling & Stock Rotation (FIFO)
body: Good stock control isn't just about saving money (though it does) — it's a food safety essential. Serve something past its use-by date and you could make a guest seriously ill, as well as breaking the law. Two simple habits keep us safe: clear date labelling and proper stock rotation.

FIFO is the golden rule of rotation: First In, First Out. When you put a delivery away, place the newer stock BEHIND the older stock, so the older items get used first and nothing gets lost at the back until it's gone off. It's a tiny habit that dramatically cuts both waste and risk.

Know your dates. A 'use-by' date is about SAFETY — never use or serve food after its use-by date, full stop. A 'best-before' date is about QUALITY — the food may be past its best but is generally still safe. When you open or prepare something, label it with the date so everyone knows how fresh it is and when it needs using.

Check dates as part of your routine and remove anything that's out of date or looks unfit, recording what you've thrown away. If you're ever unsure whether something is still good, don't gamble with a guest's health — when in doubt, throw it out and tell your supervisor.

title: Pest Awareness
body: Pests — rodents, insects, birds — aren't just unpleasant; they spread disease, contaminate food, and can get a business closed down by environmental health. The best defence is prevention and early action, and every one of us has a part to play just by being observant and tidy.

Learn the warning signs so you can catch a problem early: droppings, gnaw marks on packaging or fittings, greasy smear marks along walls, nesting material, dead insects, or an unusual musty smell. Spotting these early, before an infestation takes hold, makes them far easier and cheaper to deal with.

Prevention comes down to denying pests the three things they need: food, water and shelter. Store all food covered and off the floor, clear food debris and waste promptly (especially overnight), keep bin areas clean with lids closed, and don't leave standing water around. Keep external doors and windows closed or screened, and help seal up gaps and holes where you can.

If you see any sign of pests — or an actual pest — report it to a manager straight away. Don't keep quiet hoping it'll go away, and don't try to tackle a serious problem yourself; we use professional pest control for that. Quick, honest reporting is what stops a small issue becoming a big, expensive one.

title: Waste, Recycling & Broken Glass
body: Handling waste is a daily job, and doing it well matters for two reasons: safety and the environment. Bins hide sharp and broken items, waste attracts pests if it's not managed, and sorting it correctly helps us cut what goes to landfill. A few simple rules keep it safe and responsible.

The biggest safety rule: NEVER put your hand into a bin. You can't see what's in there, and a hidden piece of broken glass, a knife or a skewer can cause a deep cut. If something needs pushing down, use a tool, not your hand — and never overfill bins so that sharp things stick out of the top.

Broken glass deserves special care. Never pick it up with your bare hands — sweep it up with a brush and dustpan, wrap it, and put it in the designated broken-glass bin or a clearly labelled sturdy container, kept separate from general waste. Behind the bar, glass breakages happen fast, so clear the area, warn people, and never use a glass to scoop ice.

For the environment, sort waste into the correct streams — general, mixed recycling, glass, and used cooking oil into its proper container (never down the drain). Keep bin areas clean and lids closed to deter pests. Small habits from everyone add up to a safer, greener venue.

title: PPE — Personal Protective Equipment
body: PPE — Personal Protective Equipment — is the gear that protects you from a hazard: gloves, aprons, eye protection, cut-resistant gloves, non-slip footwear, and so on. It's important to understand that PPE is the LAST line of defence. We always try to remove or reduce a hazard first; PPE is there to protect you from what's left.

That means PPE only works if you actually use it, and use it correctly, for the task it's meant for. Wearing chemical gloves for a strong cleaning product, cut-resistant gloves for certain knife or slicer tasks, or eye protection where there's a splash risk — these aren't optional extras when the job calls for them.

Before you use PPE, give it a quick check: is it clean, in good condition, and the right size for you? Damaged gloves with holes, or a mask that doesn't fit, won't protect you properly. Ill-fitting or worn-out PPE can give a false sense of safety, which is almost worse than none at all.

If your PPE is damaged, worn out or missing, report it so it can be replaced — don't just carry on without it or make do. And remember, PPE supports safe working; it doesn't replace it. Wear the right kit, look after it, and it'll look after you.

title: Telephone & Enquiry Handling
body: The phone is very often a guest's very first contact with Black Horse Beamish — a wedding enquiry, a table booking, a question about a stay. That first impression is formed in seconds, and a warm, professional call can be the difference between winning that booking and losing it to somewhere that answered better.

Answer promptly — within a few rings — with a clear, friendly greeting and the venue name, so the caller knows they've reached the right place. And here's a genuine tip: smile while you speak. It sounds odd, but a smile really does carry down the line and makes you sound warm and welcoming rather than flat.

Then listen properly and take accurate notes. Get the key details — what they want, dates, numbers — and repeat them back to confirm you've got them right. Always take the caller's name and a contact number so nothing is lost, and never leave an enquiry hanging: either answer it fully or tell them exactly who will get back to them and when.

Follow up when you say you will, and make sure enquiries — especially for weddings and events — are logged properly so they don't slip through the cracks. A missed or forgotten enquiry is a lost booking and a poor impression. Handle the call well and you've started the guest's whole experience on a high.

title: Welcoming & Seating Guests
body: The welcome sets the tone for a guest's entire visit. People decide how they feel about a place within moments of walking in, so a warm, prompt greeting is worth its weight in gold. A guest who feels genuinely welcomed relaxes and enjoys themselves; one who's left standing awkwardly at the door does not.

So greet arriving guests promptly, with eye contact and a smile, and make them feel expected. Even if you're mid-task and can't seat them that second, acknowledge them — a friendly 'Welcome! I'll be right with you' works wonders. Nobody likes to feel invisible, and being noticed is the first thing a good welcome does.

When seating, a little thought goes a long way. Check the booking, and consider each guest's needs — an accessible table for someone with limited mobility, a highchair for a family, a quieter corner for an older couple. Guide them to the table, help with coats or bags if appropriate, present the menus and mention any specials.

Throughout, read the guest. Some want a chat; others just want to settle in quietly. Being welcoming isn't about being over-the-top — it's about making everyone feel expected, valued and looked after from the very first moment. Get the welcome right and the rest of the visit tends to follow.

title: Handling Difficult Customers
body: Now and then you'll meet a guest who's angry, rude or hard to please. It's part of the job, and how you handle it makes all the difference — a difficult moment handled well can actually turn a situation around, while the wrong response makes it spiral. The first rule is: don't take it personally, and stay calm.

Calm is contagious — and so is anger. Keep your voice steady and low, keep your body language open and non-confrontational, and let the guest have their say without interrupting. Very often people just want to feel heard. Acknowledge how they feel ('I can see why that's frustrating') and show that you genuinely want to help.

Focus on what you CAN do rather than what you can't. Offer a solution where you're able to, and if it's beyond your authority, don't dig in — escalate to a manager. Knowing your limits and bringing in help isn't failure; it's exactly the right move. Never argue to 'win', because winning an argument with a guest usually loses the guest.

There's a firm line, though: if a guest becomes abusive, threatening or aggressive, you do not have to stand there and take it. Get a manager, don't retaliate, and remove yourself from danger if you need to. Staying calm, listening and knowing when to escalate keeps both you and the situation safe.

title: Table Service Standards
body: Polished table service is one of those things guests notice without quite knowing why — it just feels like they're being properly looked after. It's built from a set of simple, consistent standards that any of us can deliver once we know them. Consistency is the key word: the same high standard at every table, every shift.

There's an etiquette to serving and clearing that's worth knowing. As a general rule, serve food from the guest's left and clear from the right, and pour drinks from the right — though the golden rule is simply to do it smoothly and without reaching across a guest. Carry plates and trays safely and never overload yourself; a dropped tray is dramatic and dangerous.

The 'check back' is a small habit with a big impact: a minute or two after the food lands, return to make sure everything is right — 'How's everything tasting?' It catches a problem while it's still easily fixable, and it shows guests you care. Keep the table tidy throughout, clearing finished plates, empties and crumbs so it never feels neglected.

Above all, be attentive without hovering. Read the table, anticipate what's needed — a refill, another round, the bill — and be there at the right moment without breathing down their necks. Get these standards right consistently and guests leave feeling genuinely well looked after, which is exactly what brings them back.

title: Upselling & Suggestive Selling
body: Upselling has a bad reputation, but done well it isn't pushy at all — it's simply helping guests enjoy their visit more while gently growing the bill. A genuine suggestion at the right moment ('our sticky toffee pudding is famous, shall I bring one to share?') often lands as great service, not a sales pitch.

The foundation is knowing your menu and drinks inside out. You can't recommend what you don't know, so learn the dishes, the specials, the wines and the cocktails, and know which go well together. When you can speak with genuine enthusiasm about something, guests trust the recommendation and are far more likely to say yes.

Timing and relevance matter. Suggest a starter or a side while they're choosing mains, a better wine to match the food, a dessert or coffee at the right moment. Use appetising, descriptive language — 'warm, gooey and served with clotted cream' beats 'do you want dessert?' every time. And read the guest: suggest, don't pressure.

Finally, always respect a 'no' gracefully — a cheerful 'no problem at all' keeps the mood right and leaves the door open next time. Upselling should always improve the guest's experience first; the extra spend follows naturally when it's done with genuine care rather than a hard sell.

title: Wedding & Event Day Excellence
body: For a couple, their wedding is one of the most important days of their entire lives — and they've chosen us to make it perfect. That's a real privilege and a real responsibility. Preparation is everything. Present the room immaculately and present yourself the same way; you're part of the picture in their memories and photographs.

During the day, stay one step ahead. Anticipate what's coming next so you're ready before you're needed, communicate calmly and clearly with the kitchen and the rest of the team, and keep the couple and their key people informed without fuss. Smooth teamwork is what makes a complex day look easy.

And when something goes wrong — because occasionally it will — solve it discreetly. The couple and their guests should never see the stress; they should just see a beautiful, seamless day. Fix problems quietly, keep smiling, and lean on your team. Get it right and you'll have helped create memories a couple keeps for a lifetime.

title: Responsible Alcohol Service & Spotting Intoxication
body: Serving alcohol responsibly is a legal duty and a big part of keeping our guests safe. It is against the law to sell alcohol to someone who is already drunk, and it's on us to spot when someone has had enough and to handle it well. It protects the guest, protects other guests, and protects our licence.

Learn to read the signs of intoxication: slurred or loud speech, unsteadiness on their feet, glazed or unfocused eyes, becoming argumentative or overly friendly, fumbling with money, or drinks going untouched. It's a judgement call, and it's better to notice early and slow things down than to wait until there's a problem.

When someone's had too much, handle it with tact. Slow down or stop serving them alcohol, offer water, soft drinks, or food, and do it discreetly and without embarrassing them — a friendly, respectful approach is far more likely to be accepted. Never let an intoxicated person buy drinks for others (that's a way round the refusal), and be firm but kind.

Look after their welfare too. Keep an eye on anyone who seems vulnerable, help arrange a taxi or a safe way home where you can, and never let someone drink-drive if you can prevent it. If a situation starts to escalate or someone gets aggressive, don't handle it alone — call a manager. Record any refusal in the log.

title: Lone Working Safety
body: There'll be times you're working on your own — opening up early, closing down late, cleaning a quiet area, or being the only one in the office. Lone working isn't banned, but it needs a bit of extra thought, because if something goes wrong there's no colleague right there to help.

The most important thing is that someone knows. Make sure another person knows you're on site and roughly when you expect to finish, and agree a way to check in. Keep a phone on you at all times so you can raise the alarm and be contacted, and make sure you know how you'd get help quickly if you needed it.

Keep yourself secure. When you're alone, keep external doors secured and don't let unknown callers in — deliveries and visitors can wait or be verified. Avoid the higher-risk tasks when you're on your own: things like cellar drops, working at height, or handling large amounts of cash are much better done when someone else is around.

And remember the golden rule: your personal safety always comes before the premises, the stock or the takings. If you ever feel unsafe or threatened, remove yourself from the situation and call for help — don't try to be a hero to protect property. Sensible precautions mean you can work alone safely and confidently.

title: Gas Safety Awareness
body: Gas is a brilliant tool in a kitchen but it demands respect — a gas leak can lead to fire, explosion or poisoning from carbon monoxide, which is especially dangerous because it's invisible and has no smell. This trainer is about awareness: knowing the warning signs and exactly what to do, not about doing gas work, which is strictly for registered engineers only.

Natural gas is given a distinctive 'rotten eggs' smell so leaks can be detected. So learn to recognise that smell, and know where the gas shut-off valves and the meter are before you ever need them. Other warning signs include a pilot light that keeps going out, lazy yellow or orange flames instead of crisp blue ones, or sooty marks around appliances.

If you smell gas or suspect a leak, act immediately and in the right order. Do NOT touch electrical switches or use any naked flames — a spark could ignite the gas. Ventilate the area by opening doors and windows, turn off the gas supply at the valve if it's safe to do so, evacuate, and call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999.

Only Gas Safe registered engineers may install, service or repair gas appliances — never attempt it yourself or ask an unqualified person to. Report any fault, unusual smell, or appliance that isn't working right straight away. Treat gas with respect and awareness, and it stays the useful, safe tool it should be.

title: Safe Stacking & Storage
body: How we stack and store things might seem trivial, but poor storage causes a surprising number of injuries — from items falling on people to blocked walkways and toppling stacks. A tidy, well-organised store isn't just nicer to work in; it's genuinely safer and saves time too.

Think about weight and height. Store heavier items at around waist height, where they're easy to lift without bending low or reaching high, and keep lighter items up top. Don't stack things too high or lean stacks against each other, because that's how a whole shelf comes down on someone. Take from the top of a stack, and use proper steps for high shelves rather than climbing.

Keep it clear. Stock should be off the floor (on shelving or racking) and never left blocking walkways, doorways or — most importantly — fire exits, even briefly. A box left in a corridor is a trip hazard and could block an escape route in an emergency.

Look after your shelving too. Don't overload shelves beyond what they're rated for, and report any that are damaged, wobbly or overloaded so they can be fixed before they fail. Heavy low, light high, stacks stable, routes clear — follow those and your store stays a safe place to work.

title: DSE — Office Workstation Setup
body: If you spend time working at a computer — bookings, admin, emails, rotas — how you set up your workstation really matters. Poorly set up 'Display Screen Equipment' (DSE) can lead to back, neck and shoulder aches, wrist problems and eye strain over time. A few adjustments make all the difference and cost nothing.

Start with your chair. Adjust it so your forearms are roughly horizontal when typing and your feet are flat on the floor (use a footrest if they don't reach). Sit back in the chair so your lower back is supported, and relax your shoulders rather than hunching them up around your ears.

Now the screen. Position it about an arm's length away, with the top of the screen roughly at eye level so you're not craning your neck up or down. Keep your wrists straight and relaxed while typing and using the mouse, rather than bent up or resting on a hard edge.

Finally, move. Even the perfect setup isn't meant to be held rigidly for hours — take regular short breaks, change position, and look away from the screen into the distance now and then to rest your eyes. If you get persistent aches or discomfort, report it so your workstation can be assessed and adjusted. Small habits protect you long term.

title: How to be a Great Team
body: Hospitality is the ultimate team sport. On a busy night, no one gets through it alone — it takes the kitchen, the bar, front of house, housekeeping and management all pulling in the same direction. When the team clicks, work is more enjoyable, service is better, and guests can feel the good atmosphere. So being a great team member is a skill worth taking seriously.

It starts with communication. Share information clearly — a table's running late, we're low on a dish, a big group just walked in — so everyone can adjust. A quick heads-up between departments prevents most of the little disasters that make a shift stressful. Don't assume someone else knows; tell them.

Then there's mucking in. When it's slammed, jump in and help where it's needed, even if it's 'not your job' — running a plate, clearing a table, grabbing glasses from the bar. Be reliable: turn up on time, ready to work, so your colleagues aren't left covering for you. Reliability is one of the most respected qualities in any team.

Finally, look after each other. Give and take feedback positively, treat everyone with respect, celebrate the wins together, and notice when a colleague is struggling or having a rough day. A team that supports each other handles pressure better and sticks together. We genuinely succeed — or struggle — together.

title: Conflict De-escalation
body: Sometimes tempers flare — between guests, or towards staff — and knowing how to calm a situation down is a genuinely valuable skill that keeps everyone safe. De-escalation is about taking the heat out of a moment before it becomes something worse, and most of it comes down to how you carry yourself.

Your own manner sets the tone. Stay calm and keep your voice low, steady and unhurried — shouting back or matching someone's aggression just pours fuel on the fire. Keep your body language open and non-threatening: hands visible, a relaxed stance, and a respectful distance. Never square up, point, or get in someone's face.

Then listen and acknowledge. People often escalate because they feel unheard, so letting them speak and saying something like 'I hear you, let's sort this out' can take a lot of the heat out. Avoid arguing, mocking, or issuing ultimatums — instead, offer choices where you can, which gives the person a sense of control and a way to back down without losing face.

Know your limits and when to step away. If someone is becoming violent or you feel unsafe, don't try to win — withdraw, get help, and get a manager. If there's a genuine threat of violence, call 999. Staying calm, listening, giving space and choices, and knowing when to get help keeps both you and everyone around you safe.

title: Deep Fat Fryer & Hot Oil Safety
body: The deep fat fryer is one of the most dangerous pieces of kit in any kitchen. The oil runs at around 180°C — hot enough to cause a severe, deep burn instantly — and if it catches fire, it's a fast, frightening blaze. Almost every fryer injury and fire is preventable with care and the right habits.

Water and hot oil are a deadly combination. Even a small amount of water hitting hot oil causes it to spit violently and can trigger an explosion of hot oil and steam. So make sure food going into the fryer is as dry as possible, lower baskets in gently rather than dropping them, and never let water anywhere near the oil.

Don't overfill the fryer with oil or food, keep the surrounding area clear, and never, ever try to move a fryer that's full of hot oil — wait until it has fully cooled before draining, filtering or cleaning it. Cleaning a fryer while the oil is still hot is a classic cause of serious burns.

If a fryer or oil ever catches fire, do NOT throw water on it — that will make it explode. Turn off the heat if you can do so safely, smother the flames with a fire blanket, and if it's not immediately controllable, raise the alarm, evacuate and call 999. Know where the fire blanket is before you ever need it.

title: Legionella & Water Hygiene Awareness
body: As a hotel with showers, taps and a hot tub, we have to take water hygiene seriously. Legionella bacteria live in water systems and can cause Legionnaires' disease — a serious, sometimes fatal, form of pneumonia. People catch it by breathing in tiny water droplets (a fine spray or mist) from things like showers, taps and spa pools, not by drinking the water.

Legionella thrives in warm, stagnant water — roughly between 20°C and 45°C — and where there's scale, rust or sludge to feed on. The way we keep it in check is by controlling temperature and keeping water moving: hot water kept properly hot (above 50°C), cold water kept genuinely cold (below 20°C), and outlets used regularly so water doesn't sit still.

One of the most important practical jobs is flushing little-used outlets. If a hotel room, tap or shower hasn't been used for a while, it must be flushed through before a guest uses it — run the water to clear any stagnant water sitting in the pipes. Keeping showerheads and taps clean and descaled matters too, because scale gives bacteria somewhere to grow.

You don't need to be a specialist, but you do need to report the warning signs: cold water that runs warm, hot water that's only lukewarm, showerheads furred up with scale, or outlets that never get used. Flag these to maintenance so they can be checked. Small habits keep our water safe for everyone.

title: Norovirus & Sickness Reporting
body: Norovirus, sometimes called the 'winter vomiting bug', is extremely contagious and spreads like wildfire in busy places like ours. It takes only a tiny number of virus particles to make someone ill, and it spreads through contaminated hands, surfaces, food and even the air after someone has been sick. One unwell food handler can infect dozens of guests.

That's why the single most important rule is simple: if you have sickness or diarrhoea, do NOT come to work with food, and report it to your manager. You must be symptom-free for at least 48 hours before you return to handling food. It can feel like you're letting the team down, but coming in could shut us down and make guests seriously ill.

Handwashing is your best defence — but here's a crucial point: alcohol hand gels do NOT reliably kill norovirus. You need to wash thoroughly with soap and warm water. Gel is a top-up, not a substitute, especially when norovirus is around.

If someone is sick on the premises, it needs cleaning up properly and promptly: wear the correct PPE (gloves and apron), use the right disinfectant that's effective against viruses, clean a wide area around the spot, and dispose of everything safely. Then wash your hands thoroughly. Handled quickly and correctly, we stop an outbreak in its tracks.

title: Blood & Bodily Fluids / Sharps Safety
body: In housekeeping and cleaning you can come across blood, vomit, urine or other bodily fluids, and occasionally sharps like discarded needles. These can carry infections — including bloodborne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV — so they must be handled carefully. With the right precautions, the risk is very low.

For any spillage of blood or bodily fluids, protect yourself first: put on gloves (and an apron and eye protection if there's a splash risk). Use the correct disinfectant or a bodily-fluid spill kit if we have one, clean a generous area, and double-bag and dispose of waste and used PPE properly. Wash your hands thoroughly afterwards, even though you wore gloves.

Sharps need extra caution. If you find a needle or other sharp item — in a room, a bin or down the side of a sofa — NEVER pick it up with your bare hands. Use a tool or a sharps container, or a brush and pan, and place it in a proper sharps bin. Report every find to your manager.

If you're ever pricked or cut by a sharp, or get blood or fluid into a cut, your eyes or mouth, act straight away: encourage the wound to bleed a little, wash it well with soap and water (rinse eyes/mouth with water), cover it, and report it immediately so you can get prompt medical advice. Quick action makes a real difference.

title: Severe Bleeding — What To Do
body: Most cuts at work are minor, but occasionally — with knives, glass, or powered equipment like the grounds machinery — a wound can bleed heavily. Severe (catastrophic) bleeding can become life-threatening in just a few minutes, so knowing what to do, fast, genuinely saves lives. Stay calm; your quick action is what matters most.

The single most important action for heavy bleeding is firm, direct pressure on the wound. Press hard with a clean dressing, cloth or even your gloved hand, and keep pressing — don't keep lifting off to look. If blood soaks through, don't remove the first dressing; add another on top and keep up the pressure. Where possible, wear gloves to protect yourself.

Call 999 immediately for serious bleeding, or get someone else to while you keep pressure on. If we have a bleed-control kit and you've been trained to use it, a proper trauma dressing or tourniquet can be life-saving for a limb that won't stop bleeding — but these should only be used within your training.

Keep the casualty still and reassure them, and watch for shock (pale, cold, clammy skin, fast breathing) — lie them down and keep them warm. This trainer is about awareness and the basics; if you'd like the hands-on skills, tell your manager, as we run first-aid training. Knowing these steps means you'll act, not freeze, when it counts.

title: Grounds & Powered Equipment Safety
body: Keeping our grounds looking beautiful means using powerful equipment — mowers, strimmers, hedge trimmers, leaf blowers and chainsaws. These tools save huge amounts of time, but they can cause serious injuries in a moment's carelessness, so they demand respect, training and the right protective kit.

The first rule is competence: only use equipment you've been trained and authorised to operate. Some tools, chainsaws especially, require proper certificated training — they are not something to 'have a go' with. If you're not trained on a machine, don't use it, and never let an untrained person pick one up.

Wear the correct PPE every time — typically eye protection, ear defenders, sturdy gloves, protective boots and suitable close-fitting clothing (chainsaw work needs specialist protective trousers). Before you start, check the machine and its guards are in good order, and clear the area of people, pets and debris — thrown stones and cuttings injure bystanders as well as operators.

Refuel safely with the engine switched off and cooled, keep guards in place at all times, and never remove or defeat a safety guard. If a machine is faulty, damaged or a guard is missing, take it out of use and report it. Treat these tools with the respect they deserve and the grounds stay a safe place to work.

title: Deliveries, Vehicles & Car Park Safety
body: Our car park and delivery areas are busy places where people and vehicles mix — guest cars, delivery lorries, cellar drops and staff on foot. Vehicles reversing or manoeuvring are a genuine hazard, and being aware and predictable around them keeps everyone safe.

The golden rule is to keep people and moving vehicles apart wherever possible. Stay out of blind spots, make eye contact with drivers before crossing behind or in front of them, and never assume a reversing driver has seen you — they often can't. Use marked walkways where they exist, and wear high-visibility clothing if you're working around vehicles in low light.

During deliveries, keep the area organised. Agree where a vehicle will unload, keep routes clear, and control cages and trolleys carefully — a loaded cage can be very heavy and hard to stop, especially on a slope or ramp, so never let one run away from you. Use good manual handling for offloading and don't rush.

Watch for hazards particular to outside areas: uneven ground, ice in winter, poor lighting at night, and reversing beepers you might tune out. If you spot a problem — a blocked route, a reversing vehicle with no banksman, a dark corner — flag it. A calm, aware approach around vehicles prevents some of the most serious accidents there are.
