title: Mental Health & Wellbeing at Work
body: Hospitality is a wonderful industry to work in, but let's be honest — it can also be demanding. Long hours, late nights, busy services and dealing with people all day can take a toll on anyone's wellbeing. Looking after your mental health, and each other's, is just as important as physical safety, and it's something we take seriously here.

Learn to recognise when you, or a colleague, might be struggling. Signs can include feeling constantly exhausted or overwhelmed, becoming withdrawn or unusually irritable, losing enthusiasm, or trouble sleeping. These are normal human responses to pressure — not weaknesses — and noticing them early makes them much easier to deal with.

The most powerful thing any of us can do is talk, and listen. If you're struggling, please speak to your manager or someone you trust — you won't be judged, and we would always rather know so we can help. And if you notice a colleague seems down or overloaded, a simple 'are you okay?' and a genuine listen can mean the world.

There's always support available — your manager, your GP, and free confidential helplines like the Samaritans (116 123), who are there day and night. Small things help too: taking your breaks, staying hydrated, and looking out for one another. A team that cares about wellbeing is a stronger, happier team.

title: New & Expectant Mothers at Work
body: When a colleague is pregnant, has recently given birth, or is breastfeeding, some workplace risks that are normally minor can become more significant — and we have a legal duty to protect them. This trainer helps everyone understand why, and what to do, so we can support expectant and new mothers properly.

Certain hazards deserve a closer look during pregnancy and after birth: heavy or awkward manual handling, standing for very long periods, exposure to certain chemicals, long or night shifts and fatigue, and some food-safety risks (certain foods carry infections that are riskier in pregnancy). None of this means someone can't work — it means we adjust things sensibly.

The key step is communication. If you're pregnant or a new mother, please tell your manager as early as you feel comfortable, so we can carry out a specific risk assessment for your situation and make any reasonable adjustments — lighter duties, more breaks, changes to hours, or somewhere private to rest or express milk.

For everyone else, the message is simple: be supportive and understanding, and never make assumptions about what a colleague can or can't do — that's for them and their manager to agree. Managers must act promptly when told. Looking after new and expectant mothers is both the law and simply the decent thing to do.

title: Buffets, Carveries & Hot-Holding
body: Weddings and events often mean buffets and carveries, where food sits out on display for a while — and that's exactly the situation where food safety can slip if we're not careful. The two enemies are the temperature danger zone and contamination from lots of guests helping themselves.

Temperature is everything. Hot food on display must be kept hot — 63°C or above — and cold food kept cold, at 8°C or below. Check and record these temperatures regularly throughout the service. Food that falls out of safe temperature can only be left out for a limited time before it must be used or thrown away, so keep an eye on the clock as well as the thermometer.

Protect the food from contamination. Use sneeze screens and provide separate serving utensils for each dish so guests aren't using their hands. A really important rule: when a dish runs low, replace it with a fresh, clean container rather than topping up the old one — topping up mixes older food with new and lets bacteria build up.

Don't forget allergens on a buffet — dishes should be clearly labelled, and utensils kept with their own dish to avoid transferring allergens between them. Keep the display tidy, monitor temperatures, and swap dishes rather than topping up. Get these right and a buffet is both a joy to look at and completely safe.

title: HACCP & Food Safety Management
body: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points — it's the internationally recognised system we use to keep food safe, and by law every food business must have a food safety management system based on HACCP principles. It can sound technical, but the idea behind it is simple: work out where things could go wrong, and put checks in place to stop them.

It starts by identifying hazards — the things that could make food unsafe. These fall into three groups: biological (bacteria and viruses), chemical (like cleaning products getting into food), and physical (like glass, metal or plastic). We then pinpoint the 'critical control points' (CCPs) — the steps where a check is essential to keep food safe, such as cooking, chilling and hot-holding. Each CCP has a 'critical limit', for example cooking to a core temperature of 75°C.

Next we monitor those points — checking and recording temperatures and times — and if something falls outside the safe limits, we take corrective action, like cooking it longer, adjusting a fridge, or throwing the food away. We also keep records, because those temperature logs and cleaning diaries are our proof that food is being kept safe. Many venues run this through the 'Safer Food, Better Business' pack.

Your part in all this is vital. HACCP isn't just paperwork for the chef — it only works if everyone follows the procedures, carries out and honestly records their checks, and reports anything that isn't right, like a fridge running warm or a delivery that arrives too warm. Do your bit every day and we keep our guests safe and our food hygiene rating high.

title: Manual Handling — The Basics
body: Lifting, carrying, pushing and pulling — 'manual handling' — is part of nearly every job at Black Horse Beamish, whether it's kegs, tables, mattresses, laundry or boxes of stock. Done badly, it's one of the biggest causes of injury at work: musculoskeletal injuries (bad backs, strained shoulders) make up around a third of workplace ill-health, and they can nag for years. The good news is that a few simple basics protect you every time.

Before you lift anything, think T.I.L.E.: the Task (what am I moving, and where to?), the Individual (am I able to do this, or do I need help?), the Load (how heavy and awkward is it?), and the Environment (is the floor clear and dry, is my route clear?). If a load is too heavy or awkward, don't try to be a hero — get someone to help, or use a trolley, sack barrow or other aid.

When you do lift, follow the golden rules: plan your route first, stand close to the load with your feet slightly apart, bend your knees rather than your back, keep your back straight, get a secure grip, and lift smoothly using the power in your legs. Keep the load close to your body, and never twist while carrying — move your feet to turn instead.

A few more: don't carry so much that you can't see where you're going, set loads down carefully while watching your fingers and toes, and push rather than pull where you can. If you ever feel a strain or twinge, stop straight away and report it. These same basics apply to every lifting job you'll ever do here.

title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults
body: As a hotel, restaurant and venue we welcome all kinds of guests, including vulnerable adults — older people, people with disabilities or illness, or anyone who may be less able to protect themselves. Safeguarding means looking out for their welfare and acting if we think something is wrong. It sits alongside our work to protect children.

Abuse of a vulnerable adult can take several forms: physical, emotional, sexual, financial (someone taking their money), or neglect (not being cared for properly). Signs to be alert to include unexplained injuries, someone who seems fearful or is being controlled by another person, poor hygiene or appearing under-fed, sudden withdrawal, or being denied food, money or their own belongings.

If something concerns you, don't try to investigate or confront anyone — that's not your role and could make things worse. Instead, note down what you have actually seen or heard, factually, and report it to the Duty Manager, who will decide what to do next. If a person is in immediate danger, call 999 straight away.

Keep any concern confidential and share it only with those who need to know. You don't need to be certain, and you won't get anyone 'in trouble' by raising a genuine worry — you might be the one person who notices and speaks up for someone who can't speak up for themselves.

title: Spotting Modern Slavery
body: Modern slavery is closer than most people think, and hospitality is a higher-risk industry for it. It means people being forced to work or live against their will through threats, coercion, debt or deception — and the victims could be agency staff, contractors, people in a supplier's chain, or even guests being exploited.

There are signs worth knowing. Someone who seems under the control of another person, who doesn't hold their own ID, bank card or wages, who is always dropped off and collected, who seems fearful, withdrawn or reluctant to talk, who works very long hours, or who shows signs of neglect or poor living conditions. One or two signs may mean nothing — but a pattern is worth noticing.

If you suspect someone is being exploited, do NOT confront the person you think is controlling them, and don't put yourself or the potential victim at risk. Quietly report your concern to the Duty Manager or General Manager, who can take it further.

In an emergency where someone is in immediate danger, call 999. Otherwise concerns can be reported to the Modern Slavery Helpline on 08000 121 700. Trust your instincts — spotting and reporting the signs could help free someone from a terrible situation.

title: Choking — What To Do
body: Where food and drink are served, choking can happen — and knowing what to do in those few seconds can save a life. The first thing to work out is whether it's mild or severe. If the person can still cough, speak or breathe, it's mild: encourage them to keep coughing, which is the most effective way to shift the blockage. Don't slap their back at this stage.

If it's severe — they can't speak, cough or breathe, may be clutching their throat, going red then blue — you need to act immediately. Lean them forward and give up to five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking after each one to see if it's cleared.

If back blows don't work, give up to five abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, place a fist just above the belly button, grasp it with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards. Keep alternating five back blows and five abdominal thrusts.

Call 999 (or get someone to) if the blockage doesn't clear quickly or the person becomes unresponsive — if they collapse, start CPR. Even after a severe choking episode that clears, especially if abdominal thrusts were used, the person should be checked by a medical professional. Stay calm — you knowing these steps could be the difference.

title: CPR & Defibrillator (AED) Awareness
body: A cardiac arrest is when someone's heart suddenly stops and they become unresponsive and aren't breathing normally. It can happen to anyone, any age. It's a true emergency: for every minute without CPR and a defibrillator, the chance of survival falls by around 10%, so acting fast really does save lives.

If you find someone collapsed and not breathing normally: call 999 immediately (put it on speaker), and send someone to fetch the nearest defibrillator (AED). Then start CPR straight away — push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about 5–6cm deep, at a rate of 100–120 pushes a minute (the beat of 'Stayin' Alive' is about right). If you're trained, give two rescue breaths after every 30 compressions; if not, hands-only CPR is fine and still saves lives.

A defibrillator (AED) is designed for anyone to use — you don't need training. Turn it on and it talks you through everything: attach the pads to the person's bare chest as shown, and it will check the heart and tell you if a shock is needed. Make sure nobody is touching the person when it delivers a shock.

Keep going — CPR and the AED — until the emergency services arrive and take over, or the person starts to show signs of life. Don't worry about doing it 'perfectly': doing something is far better than doing nothing.

title: Phishing & Cyber-Security Awareness
body: Most cyber-attacks on a business don't start with a genius hacker — they start with a scam message that tricks a person. It's called 'phishing': an email, text or call pretending to be someone trustworthy (a bank, a supplier, even the boss) to steal passwords or money, or to get you to open something that infects our systems.

Learn the warning signs: a sense of urgency ('act now or else'), an unexpected attachment or link, a sender address that's slightly wrong, poor spelling or odd wording, or a request to change bank/payment details or send money. If a message feels off, it probably is.

The golden rules: don't click links or open attachments you weren't expecting; never enter your password after following a link in a message; and always verify any request to change bank details or make a payment by contacting the person a different way (a known phone number), not by replying. Fraudsters love to redirect supplier payments this way.

Also: never share your passwords, use strong and different passwords for different things, lock your screen when you step away, and report anything suspicious to your manager straight away — even if you already clicked. Fast reporting lets us limit any damage. When in doubt, don't click — ask.

title: Speaking Up (Whistleblowing)
body: Sometimes you might become aware of something seriously wrong at work — and speaking up about it is one of the most important things you can do. 'Whistleblowing' is raising a genuine concern about wrongdoing, and the law specifically protects people who do it in good faith.

The sorts of things to speak up about include: theft or fraud, a danger to health, safety or food safety, harm or risk to a guest, child or vulnerable adult, a serious breach of the law, damage to the environment, or someone deliberately covering any of these up. It's different from a personal complaint about your own job, which should go through the grievance procedure.

You should normally raise a concern with your manager or the General Manager. If that's not appropriate — for example if it involves them — you can raise it with the business owners. You don't need cast-iron proof; you just need to genuinely believe something is wrong.

Concerns raised in good faith are taken seriously and handled as confidentially as possible, and nobody will be victimised or treated badly for speaking up. Staying silent can let real harm continue — so if something isn't right, please say something.

title: Energy & Water — Reducing Our Impact
body: Being greener isn't just good for the planet — it cuts our running costs too, and lots of small habits from everyone add up to a big difference. Energy and water are two of the easiest places to make an impact, and it mostly comes down to not wasting what we don't need.

For energy: switch off lights, equipment and appliances when they're not in use, rather than leaving them on or on standby. Close external doors and windows when the heating or air-con is running, don't overfill the kettle, and make sure fridges and freezers seal properly and aren't left open. Turn things off properly at the end of service.

For water: don't leave taps running, report dripping taps and leaks promptly (a dripping tap wastes a surprising amount), only run dishwashers and washing machines with full loads, and use the right amount rather than the most. In the kitchen and cellar, mop up and manage water sensibly.

And keep an eye out generally: report faults like leaks, broken seals, or heating and lighting left on in empty areas. None of this is complicated — it's just being switched-on (and switching things off!). Every little bit helps our costs and our environmental footprint.

title: Anaphylaxis & Adrenaline Auto-injectors
body: Anaphylaxis is the most severe kind of allergic reaction — it's life-threatening and can develop within minutes. This trainer sits alongside our allergen work: getting allergens right prevents reactions, but everyone guest-facing should also know how to recognise and respond to one, because seconds count.

Know the signs: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; difficulty breathing, wheezing or a hoarse voice; a widespread rash or hives; feeling faint, dizzy or suddenly very unwell; and collapse. If a guest tells you they're having a reaction, believe them and act — don't wait to 'see how it goes'.

If you suspect anaphylaxis, call 999 immediately and say the word 'anaphylaxis'. If the person has their own adrenaline auto-injector (such as an EpiPen), help them use it without delay — it's given firmly into the outer thigh (it works through clothing) and held in place for the required few seconds. A second dose can be given after 5 minutes if there's no improvement and another injector is available.

Keep the person still — lying down with legs raised, or sitting up if they're struggling to breathe — and do NOT stand them up or let them walk, as this can be dangerous. Stay with them until help arrives. Fast action with adrenaline saves lives.

title: Cash, Card & Payment Security
body: Handling payments carefully protects our guests from fraud and protects us from losses and card-data theft. Card payments come with rules (the 'PCI' standards), but most of it is common sense: treat card details like the sensitive information they are.

Never write down or store a guest's full card number, and never take a photo of a card or email card details — that's exactly what fraudsters want. Handle a customer's card as little as possible, ideally letting them tap or insert it themselves. Be alert to anything odd about a card or the person using it, and refer concerns to a manager.

Look after the card machines too: check them for signs of tampering or an extra device attached (a 'skimmer'), and report anything that looks wrong. Refunds, voids and manual key-entry should be authorised by a supervisor or manager, which protects you as well as the business.

With cash, count and handle it discreetly and out of guests' sight, follow the cash-handling procedure, and report any suspected fraud, counterfeit notes or discrepancies straight away. A little care at the payment stage stops a lot of problems later.

title: Front Desk Security & Suspicious Behaviour
body: Reception is the front line of our security — often the first place a problem would show itself. Being welcoming and being security-aware go hand in hand: most people are exactly who they say they are, but staying switched-on protects our guests, our team and our building.

A golden rule: never reveal a guest's room number or confirm whether someone is staying with us. If someone asks to be let into a room or wants a guest's details, verify they are that guest (or have permission) first. Control room keys and keycards carefully, and watch for 'tailgating' — someone slipping through a door into staff-only or guest areas behind you.

Be alert to suspicious behaviour: someone loitering, avoiding eye contact or staff, asking unusual questions about security, rooms or guests, or trying doors. Trust your instincts — if something feels off, it's worth a second look. You can challenge politely ('Can I help you find something?') or, if you're unsure, quietly alert a manager.

And unattended bags or packages: don't touch or move them — keep people away and report to a manager, who'll decide what to do. A friendly, observant front desk keeps the whole venue safer without ever feeling unwelcoming.

title: Linen & Laundry Safety
body: Handling linen looks harmless, but it hides several real risks — so a bit of care keeps housekeeping safe. The biggest surprise hazard is sharp objects hidden in bed linen and towels: guests occasionally leave needles, razors, broken glass or other sharps wrapped up in the sheets.

Because of that, never plunge your hands into a bundle of linen or press it down into a bag or trolley. Strip beds carefully and watch what you're doing, and treat soiled linen especially cautiously — wear gloves, and handle it as though it could be contaminated, because it can carry bacteria or bodily fluids. If you find a sharp, don't grab it: report it and follow the sharps procedure.

Then there's manual handling: wet laundry is heavy, so use trolleys, don't overload them, and lift bags using good technique rather than dragging or hauling. Keep trolleys under control on slopes and in lifts.

Finally, the laundry area itself has hot machines, irons and chemicals. Beware hot surfaces and steam, follow the machine instructions, use laundry chemicals safely (COSHH), and keep the area tidy to avoid slips and trips. A careful approach makes light work of the linen.

title: Guest Room Security & Privacy
body: Guests trust us with their private space and their belongings, and protecting that trust is a core part of the job. It comes down to two things: keeping rooms secure, and respecting guests' privacy.

On security, keys and keycards are the priority — never lend yours, never leave them lying around, and keep master keys especially secure. Never let anyone into a guest's room unless you've verified they are the guest staying there; a polite check protects everyone. And never tell anyone a guest's room number or confirm who is staying.

On privacy, always knock and announce yourself before entering a room, and respect 'do not disturb' signs. Don't touch or move guests' belongings any more than the job needs, and never look through, borrow or comment on their possessions. What you see in a room stays private — don't discuss or share it, and definitely never on social media.

If you do come across something concerning in a room — signs a guest may be vulnerable or unwell, weapons, drugs, or anything that worries you — don't ignore it: report it to your manager, who'll decide what to do. Respect and discretion are what make guests feel safe with us.

title: Hand & Power Tool Safety
body: Hand and power tools make maintenance work quick and effective, but they cause serious injuries when they're misused or poorly maintained. The foundation is simple: only use tools you've been trained and are competent to use, and always use the right tool for the job — improvising with the wrong tool is a common cause of accidents.

Inspect tools before you use them. Look for damage — cracked casings, frayed cables, blunt or chipped blades, loose heads — and take anything faulty out of use and report it. Make sure guards are fitted and working, and never remove or defeat a guard to work faster.

Wear the right PPE for the task — eye protection is a must for anything that cuts, grinds or drills, plus gloves, ear defenders and dust protection where needed. Secure the workpiece (for example in a clamp) rather than holding it by hand, and keep your hands and body clear of the cutting line.

With power tools, disconnect from the power before changing blades, bits or discs, keep cables clear of the work and walkways, never carry a tool by its cable, and let cutting tools stop completely before putting them down. Store tools safely and keep them clean and sharp. Respect them and they'll serve you well.

title: Hot Tub & Spa Safety
body: Our hot tub is a lovely feature for guests, but warm water is the perfect breeding ground for harmful bacteria — including Legionella and Pseudomonas — which can make people seriously ill if the water isn't properly controlled. Managing it safely is essential, not optional.

The key is water quality. Keep the disinfectant (chlorine or bromine) and pH at the correct levels, and test and record them regularly throughout the day — a spa pool needs checking far more often than a swimming pool because it's warm and heavily used. Follow the cleaning and maintenance schedule, and if the water ever goes cloudy, smells off, or the readings are wrong, take the tub out of use and report it.
Handle the spa chemicals safely: they're hazardous (COSHH), so use the right PPE, follow the instructions, store them correctly, and never mix them — mixing spa chemicals can release dangerous gas.

Don't forget the physical safety around the tub: wet surfaces are slippery, so manage slip risks, and make sure the safety signage is clear and in place — water temperature, no diving, no glass, supervise children, and cautions for pregnancy or medical conditions. Respect the water chemistry and the tub is a safe pleasure for guests.
